reasoning: The extract gives a fair amount on evaluation, so it clears Level 1. It says the Government will evaluate the effects of the rises to 66 and 67 before 68 takes effect, and will analyse the equalisation to 65 and the rise from 65 to 66 "which will provide additional evidence to help the Government to assess the best course of action". It gives a timetable: the next review "will conclude by 2023", and the legislation requires it "by July 2023". It gives a reason: to consider the latest life expectancy projections and allow "adequate notice". It also lists outcome measures under Fuller Working Lives: employment rate of over-50s by age band and gender, average age of labour market exit, and the employment gap between 50–64 and 35–49 year olds. These are described as letting "individuals, employers, stakeholders and Government" track progress. The commitment to "monitor the effects of State Pension age rises alongside the reforms" adds to this. That reaches Level 2: there are measures, plans for evaluation, and a timetable. It falls short of Level 3 for three reasons. First, the evaluation is not specified: there is no method, no named outcomes tied to State Pension age itself, and no body responsible. Second, nothing says what happens to the results or how they will be published. The strongest counter-example to Level 2 is that the Fuller Working Lives indicators are not clearly linked to the SPA rise and that there is no testing, though evaluation is covered. To reach Level 3 the document would have to explain how the evaluation will be done, which outcomes it will assess, and when and where the results will be published. It would also need to say how they will feed into the decision on 68. There is also no mention of consultation.
